o: Repeatedly: if the front element is the current minimum, remove it (1 op); otherwise rotate it to the back (1 op). Count total operations until empty. For [3,4,-1] the answer is 5. Simulation with a deque is O(n²) — too slow for n = 1e5. Instead process values in increasing order and count, for each removal, how many alive elements lie cyclically between the current head and the target position.
k: Elements leave in increasing value order; the head after removing position p becomes the next alive position after p (wrapping around).
The cost of removing the next-smallest value at original position p equals the number of alive positions encountered from the head up to p, cyclically.
A Fenwick tree over original indices supports both 'count alive in a range' and 'find the t-th alive position' in O(log n).

a.n: Approach 1: Sort by value + Fenwick tree
a.i: Initialize a BIT with 1 at every index (all alive). Process elements in increasing value order. For the element at original index p (1-indexed q = p+1): if q ≥ head, cost = alive-in[head..q]; else cost = alive-in[head..n] + alive-in[1..q]. Add the cost, kill position q in the BIT, and set head to the next alive position after q (wrapping to the global first alive if none).
s: Pair each value with its index and sort ascending.
Build a Fenwick tree of all-ones and helpers: prefix query, point update, and k-th-alive select via binary search.
For each element in value order, compute the cyclic alive count from head to its position and add it to the answer.
Remove the position and advance head to its alive successor (with wrap-around); return the total.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting plus O(log n) BIT operations per element (query, update, and binary-searched select).
a.sp: O(n) for the Fenwick tree and the sorted index array.

w: The mental model: imagine the array as a circular list; removing the i-th smallest costs the cyclic distance (in alive elements) from the head. Verifying against [3,4,-1]: costs 3 (rotate 3, rotate 4, remove −1), then 1, then 1 → 5. Pitfalls: 1-indexing the BIT consistently, the wrap-around head update, and using 64-bit answers (up to ~n²/2 ≈ 5·10⁹). A follow-up: what if duplicates existed — break ties by index to preserve determinism.
